book: Therigatha — Verses of the Elder Nuns

1: I was born in a virtuous family, but I was unlucky and poor. A woman with a husband's consent, I suffered in the world of service, and old age came to me while I served the wives of others. Then I met the wanderers, and I went forth — and in this going-forth I have known the freedom for which I left everything.

Old am I now, and gaunt; with a staff I make my way to the park. And there, having set down my cloak and bowl, I sat beneath a tree — and the freedom of the heart came to me, and I saw the causes of things, and I rejoiced. O bliss! O bliss! The three fires are out.

Washing my feet, I saw the water flow; and I reflected: so the body goes, by stages, to decay. And taking that as my theme, I sat in the night, and before morning the darkness of ignorance was gone, and I saw the break of a day that will not end.
2: A young man, following the nun Subha on the road, said: You have eyes like a fawn's — why hide them? And Subha answered: What you desire is a bowl of filth; what you desire is a vessel of disease, a heap of sores, a construct, a mirage. Eyes like mine will one day be food for worms. If you doubt me, come — take them now from my hand. And the young man begged her pardon, and she gave it.

A brahmin taunted Soma: That which the sages of renown have attained — that state is hard for a woman to reach, for her wisdom is small. And Soma answered: What matters the woman's state of mind, when she has set her heart on the teaching? Whether I am a woman or a man — what is that to me? In the mind that knows freedom there is no woman and no man, only the freedom.
3: My husband dead on the road, my two sons dead in the flood, my parents and brother dead in the burning city — I came to the charnel ground, and I knew the world for what it is. I watched a river fill and empty; I watched a woman plant seeds and weeds return; and in the watching, the grain of the teaching opened. I gathered the ends of my robe, and I was free.

The flood took my little one, the vulture took my eldest, the fire took my house; and I sat down on the bank of my grief with nothing left to lose. That is where the path begins: at the bank of the flood, with nothing left to lose.

At the end of my days I looked back on it all — the houses, the sons, the fires, the floods — and I said: All compounded things are perishing; that is the word of the awakened. Heeding it, I was at peace. And the sisters who found me said: She who suffered most has gone out like a lamp that has finished its oil — quietly, and in light.
